claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the formation and self-healing ability of a mechanically robust passive oxide layer.
The multi-element nature of high-entropy alloys promotes formation of a complex, stable oxide film.
The passive oxide film can rapidly repair itself after mechanical disruption.
Rapid repair of the passive film reduces localized corrosion.
Rapid repair of the passive film reduces wear-induced degradation.
The proposed initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous distribution of constituent elements.
Controlled surface pretreatment can thicken or stabilize the passive film.
Environmental conditions can be altered to favor rapid passive-film formation.
Passive-film integrity, thickness, adhesion, and self-healing properties mediate tribocorrosion resistance.
Rapid film reformation limits exposure of the underlying metal to corrosive agents.
Rapid film reformation reduces initiation sites for wear.
An alloy with an enhanced, self-healing passive film will have a significantly lower wear rate than the matched untreated baseline.
An alloy with an enhanced, self-healing passive film will have a significantly lower corrosion current density than the matched untreated baseline.
Enhancing passive-film self-healing will markedly reduce combined wear-corrosion synergy.
The untreated baseline will form its passive film more slowly or form a less stable film under otherwise identical conditions.
The predicted protection should hold under moderate mechanical disruption and corrosive attack.
Extreme mechanical loads can overwhelm passive-film self-healing and cause the protective mechanism to fail.
Highly aggressive corrosive environments can overwhelm passive-film self-healing and cause the protective mechanism to fail.
The individual contributions of alloying elements to passive-film stability are not fully quantified.
The kinetics of passive-film reformation under dynamic wear-corrosion conditions are not fully quantified.

contradictions.description: The baseline and experimental design define the control as untreated, but the falsification rule refers to comparison with a 'treated baseline.'
